paper_title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot's other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot control (Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025b; Qu et al., 2025), building on robot demonstration learning (Brohan et al., 2023) and multimodal 1Code is available at franciscoliu/SAFI. 1 Figure 1: Two possible responses after takeover from the same holding state. Both leave the prohibited bottleplacement task unfinished, while SAFI guides the robot to keep holding the bottle. task grounding (Driess et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2023). Generalist policies extend these capabilities across robot platforms and unfamiliar environments (Ghosh et al., 2024; Black et al., 2025b,a), while action-sequence prediction and efficient finetuning improve manipulation performance (Zhao et al., 2023; Chi et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025a; Cui et al., 2026a). As these policies acquire more skills, deployment also requires control over which learned behaviors remain appropriate to execute. This requirement becomes concrete when context makes an otherwise feasible action hazardous. Risk can emerge as multimodal interaction develops (Liu et al., 2026), and changed semantic conditions can similarly make successful robot execution unsafe (Chen et al., 2026). VLAs may also act without meaningful instructions (Jang et al., 2026), while adversarial prompts and poisoned training data can induce harmful or attacker-chosen behaviors (Robey et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025). Withholding an executable behavior is therefore necessary complement to instruction following. Planning methods support this control through robot affordances (Ichter et al., 2023), uncertaintybased requests for help (Ren et al., 2023), and contextual safety specifications (Ravichandran et al., 2026). At the policy level, constrained learning (Zhang et al., 2025) and refusal demonstrations (Chen et al., 2026) teach safer responses. Selective unlearning offers another route by reducing unwanted behavior while preserving useful capabilities in language models (Yao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024) and VLAs (Ranjan and Polyzou, 2026; Wang et al., 2026). Since earlier actions determine later observations in sequential control (Ross et al., 2011), evaluation from initial states can leave intermediate states untested when an edited policy stops before reaching them. We examine these states by transferring control from the original policy during execution. This reveals failure to stop ongoing tasks, as several policies that suppress completion from initial states still complete the prohibited task after takeover. Even when it remains unfinished, unsafe alternative responses arise, including dropping held bottle (Figure 1). Dropping and holding both prevent placement but have different physical consequences. These observations, developed in Section 2, motivate the following research question. How can VLAs stop ongoing prohibited tasks while maintaining an appropriate physical response? Addressing this requires models to suppress prohibited behavior across execution states and produce an alternative response suited to the robots current state. To meet these requirements, we propose State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alterIts two-stage design combines Fallback native. Target Construction, which assigns holding targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, with Joint Policy Adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. By learning an explicit fallback across execution states, SAFI enables the robot to stop prohibited tasks with holding response while preserving its other skills. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. We identify failures to stop ongoing tasks and unsafe alternative responses in VLAs through an intermediate-state takeover evaluation that jointly examines prohibited execution and physical events. 2. We propose SAFI, two-stage framework that constructs fallback targets from prohibited-task demonstrations and jointly optimizes fallback and retained-task imitation to suppress prohibited behavior and learn an appropriate alternative response while preserving permitted skills. 3. We evaluate SAFI across multiple LIBERO task suites and BadLIBERO backdoor setting. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI achieves low prohibited-task completion rates after takeover with no recorded drops or falls, while preserving performance on retained tasks.

sections.title: 2 Motivations
sections.content: Failure to Stop Ongoing Tasks. Our first motivation is inspired by findings that safety-aligned language models can continue harmful responses when given their opening text, despite normally refusing such requests (Qi et al., 2025). This raises related question for VLAs about whether suppressing prohibited task also prevents its continuation once execution is underway. To examine this, we let the original policy begin task and then transfer control to policy trained to suppress it. As shown in Figure 2(a), some evaluated policies prevent prohibited stove activation from the initial state, yet activate the stove in nearly all episodes after early takeover and all episodes after mid-task takeover. These results show that suppression from initial states does not reliably prevent continuation of the same prohibited task once execution is underway. Unsafe Alternative Responses. second challenge is about what robot does when forbidden task remains unfinished. Prior work distinguishes execution failure from deliberate refusal, showing why low task success alone is an incomplete safety signal (Chen et al., 2026). Similarly, for robot already holding an object, this distinction also involves the consequences of its alternative actions. In the example shown in Figure 2(b), some evaluated policies leave the prohibited task unfinished but drop the held bottle. Both dropping the bottle and keeping it held satisfy the non-completion criterion, although their physical consequences differ. These findings reveal two challenges in enforcing behavioral prohibitions in VLAs: (1) suppression observed from initial states may fail after takeover, and (2) preventing task completion does not ensure an acceptable physical response. Addressing both challenges calls for an approach that suppresses the prohibited behavior across execution states and guides the robot toward an appropriate alternative response. 2 refusal training (Jang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: In this section, we present SAFI, two-stage framework for adapting VLAs to behavioral prohibitions. The design addresses two challenges in enforcing these prohibitions: (1) failures to stop ongoing tasks and (2) unsafe alternative responses, as identified in Section 2. Overview of SAFI. As shown in Figure 3, Fallback Target Construction assigns holding responses across prohibited-task demonstrations. Joint Policy Adaptation then learns these targets alongside the original actions for retained tasks.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate SAFIs effectiveness in suppressing prohibited behavior and preserving the robots other skills through four research questions. (1) Can SAFI suppress prohibited behavior after 4 takeover while maintaining an acceptable physical response? (2) How do the two training components in SAFI contribute to its performance? (3) Can SAFI balance target suppression with retained-task performance? (4) Does SAFI maintain the intended holding response after takeover?

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Base models. We use the released OpenVLAOFT policies (Kim et al., 2025a) as our base VLAs. These policies predict continuous action chunks from camera observations, proprioception, and language instruction. For each LIBERO prohibition, we adapt the suite-specific policy and evaluate utility on the other tasks in that suite. Baselines. The original OpenVLA-OFT policy (Kim et al., 2025a) provides reference for behavior before adaptation. Gradient Ascent (GA) increases imitation error on prohibited-task demonstrations (Maini et al., 2024). Building on this objective, Gradient Difference (GradDiff) adds retained-task imitation (Maini et al., 2024). NPORT adapts negative preference optimization to continuous actions and combines it with retained-task imitation (Zhang et al., 2024). RMU redirects hidden representations on prohibited-task inputs while matching the original representations on retained inputs (Li et al., 2024). To compare alternativeresponse supervision, Refusal FT learns homereturn actions inspired by HazardArena (Chen et al., 2026). VLA-Forget (Ranjan and Polyzou, 2026) provides VLA unlearning comparison through an OFT adaptation with module-wise updates and action distillation. Baseline adaptations are described in Appendix C.5. Benchmarks and evaluation. We evaluate tasks from LIBERO (Liu et al., 2023) that the original policy can execute and for which scripted holding passes the applicability check. These suites vary task goals, spatial relations, and object identities, respectively. After the original policy begins execution, edited policies take over from matched restored states early or midway through the task. We also test attack-target suppression in GoBAs poisoned-object BadLIBERO setting (Zhou et al., 2025), using the implanted policy as the reference. Task selection and takeover protocols are described in Appendix C.1. Evaluation metrics. Target Success Rate measures whether the prohibited target is attained after takeover. For BadLIBERO, the target is the attack objective. We also report Physical Incident Rate, which records defined physical events such as object drops, and Action Saturation Rate, which records episodes whose commands reach the controllers clipping bounds under the settings saturation criterion. Physical incidents are counted whenever they occur, including alongside target attainment. To assess the robots other skills, Retained Success Rate measures performance on permitted tasks from normal initial states. We report rates as percentages and average the evaluated Goal, Spatial, and Object settings equally for the main LIBERO score. The suite breakdown and metric equations are provided in Appendices D.1 and C.3. 4.

sections.title: Implementation Details
sections.content: We adapt SAFI using LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) on the language-model layers and jointly update the inherited action head. The LIBERO-Goal and BadLIBERO experiments use NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPUs. Training settings and checkpointselection procedures are provided in Appendix C.4.

sections.title: 4.3 Main Results
sections.content: Our first research question asks Can SAFI suppress prohibited behavior after takeover while maintaining an acceptable physical response? We address this question by comparing takeover outcomes on LIBERO and BadLIBERO in Table 1. On LIBERO, NPO-RT records Target Success Rate of 31.9% and Physical Incident Rate of 19.9%. GA and GradDiff lower target attainment further, but their high Action Saturation Rates indicate commands at the controllers clipping bounds. Refusal FT avoids this saturation but has higher average target success and physical incident rates than SAFI, with the difference driven mainly by Goal (Appendix D.1). SAFI reduces target success from the original policys 99.7% to 1.3%, with no recorded physical incidents or action-saturation episodes. The BadLIBERO results distinguish suppression from the physical response, as several methods attain zero attack-target success with different physical outcomes. NPO-RT records zero attack-target success but 22.5% Physical Incident Rate and 100.0% Action Saturation Rate, so blocking the attack leaves incidents and saturated commands. GA and GradDiff show the same pattern of complete attack suppression accompanied by physical incidents and saturation. SAFI records zero on all three endpoints, matching RMU. Refusal FT also avoids attack-target attainment and physical incidents, although 2.5% of episodes satisfy the saturation criterion. Across these settings, SAFI combines low prohibited-target attainment with an acceptable response under the measured criteria.

sections.title: 4.4 Ablation Study
sections.content: Our second question asks How do the two training components in SAFI contribute to its performance? We examine their roles on Spatial and Object by removing one imitation term at time and comparing each variant with full SAFI in Table 2. The original policy provides the reference without either term. These comparisons assess how each component affects target attainment, the physical response, and performance on permitted tasks. Removing fallback imitation. We first remove fallback imitation while keeping supervision on retained tasks. This comparison tests whether continued training on permitted behaviors also changes execution of the prohibited task. The variant preserves high retained success but reaches the prohibited target at rates of 99.7% on Spatial and 100.0% on Object, leaving ongoing execution close to that of the original policy. Physical incidents also persist, including 30.9% rate on Object. Full SAFI reduces target success to 3.4% and 0.3%, respectively, with no recorded physical incidents in either suite. The difference supports explicitly teaching the holding response to suppress ongoing execution and guide the robots behavior after takeover. Removing retained-task imitation. sections.title: 4.5 Retained-Task Utility
sections.content: The utility loss under fallback-only training leads to our third question, Can SAFI balance target suppression with retained-task performance? To examine this trade-off, we evaluate checkpoints throughout adaptation on Spatial and Object and compare their suppression and retained success in Figure 4. Each point pairs takeover suppression with performance on permitted tasks, placing policies that perform well on both measures toward the upper right. GA achieves high suppression with zero retained success at every sampled checkpoint. GradDiff improves retained success during adaptation, reaching 34.2% on Spatial and 41.7% on Object alongside high target suppression. NPO-RT and RMU exhibit the complementary trade-off, preserving high retained success at lower suppression levels. Refusal FT also reaches high suppression, although its retained success is lower than SAFIs at comparable suppression levels. The later SAFI checkpoints combine the two objectives, reaching 99.7% suppression with 97.2% retained success on Spatial and 99.0% suppression with 93.6% retained success on Object. These operating points preserve substantially more utility than GA and GradDiff at high suppression, while improving suppression over the utility-preserving NPO-RT and RMU checkpoints. Further retained-task results and checkpoint-selection details are provided in Appendix D.3.

VLA research improves manipulation through pretrained representations (Kim et al., 2025b; Qu et al., 2025), efficient action decoding (Kim et al., 2025a), and language-based action hierarchies (Belkhale et al., 2024). Safety methods add constrained policy learning (Zhang et al., 2025) and contextual planning guardrails (Ravichandran et al., 2026). Generative-model studies suppress harmful responses (Yao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024) and evaluate forgetting alongside retained utility (Maini et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025). Task arithmetic edits parameter vectors (Ilharco et al., 2023), NPO uses negative-preference optimization (Zhang et al., 2024), and RMU redirects representations (Li et al., 2024). Within VLAs, VLA-Forget selects components for editing (Ranjan and Polyzou, 2026), target-and-control auditing examines task-vector negation (Wang et al., 2026), and SOUL targets features associated with state hallucination (Lee et al., 2026). Replacement labels and refusal answers offer alternative supervision for targeted language inputs (Eldan and Russinovich, 2023; Maini et al., 2024). SAFI extends this supervision to fallback actions across execution states while preserving retained behaviors. We evaluate suppression alongside the resulting physical responses.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we address the challenges of stopping ongoing prohibited tasks and guiding VLAs toward appropriate physical responses. We propose SAFI, which first constructs holding targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations and then jointly optimizes fallback and retained-task imitation. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on selected LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks show that SAFI suppresses prohibited completion after takeover while preserving retained-task performance, with no recorded physical incidents.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Broader Deployment Settings. We evaluate OpenVLA-OFT on selected LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks using fixed training seed. Future work could extend this evaluation to additional VLA architectures and robot embodiments, with repeated training runs to assess the consistency of suppression and retained utility. Testing physical robots under varied sensing and control conditions would further clarify the approachs practical scope. More Flexible Fallback Responses. SAFI currently learns holding response for tasks that pass the applicability check. When an object is unstable or physical interaction is already underway, suitable fallback may require controlled motion. Future work could construct targets for responses such as placing an object down or withdrawing from contact, and study how to learn these responses alongside retained-task imitation.

sections.content: Algorithm 1 summarizes the two-stage procedure in Section 3. After checking that holding is an appropriate response, SAFI constructs fallback targets and jointly learns them with retained-task actions using the two imitation losses in Figure 3. B.1 Fallback Action Encoding The OFT action representation has = 7 coordinates, comprising six arm-motion coordinates and one gripper coordinate. The specialist experiments use chunks of = 8 actions. For arm coordinate j, let q01,j and q99,j be the first and ninety-ninth percentile bounds in the original policys actionnormalization statistics. Equation 1 encodes physical zero motion as The following settings support the comparisons in Section 4. C.1 Evaluation Coverage We use the released Goal, Spatial, and Object specialistson the tasks listed in Table 8. The Spatial and Object cohorts contain the first four eligible tasks in fixed candidate order. Eligibility requires successful original-policy execution, faithful restoration of takeover states, and scripted holding that prevents prohibited completion and physical incidents. Both takeover states must retain gripper contact with the same target object. Calibration and held-out evaluation use separate initial states, with normal starts for both target and retained tasks during calibration. Calibration uses ten states per task, followed by forty held-out target episodes and ten episodes on each of the other nine tasks for retained utility. The LIBERO aggregate weights Goal, Spatial, and Object equally after averaging within each suite, with the breakdown in Appendix D.1. C.2 Takeover States and Windows Successful original-policy trajectories supply matched states for every evaluated method. The early state occurs ten control steps after the first gripper-close command, and the mid-task state lies halfway between that point and task completion. Each takeover starts fresh action chunk from the edited policy. Snapshot restoration supplies creamcheese placement states, and action replay supplies the remaining states. Table 4 summarizes the observation windows, including the settings that continue after target attainment.

C.4 Training and Checkpoint Selection We adapt the OFT specialist through languagemodel LoRA and the inherited action head, keeping the remaining components frozen. The training settings for SAFI are given in Table 5, with its 300-update budget shared by GA, GradDiff, NPORT, RMU, Refusal FT, and the loss and coverage variants on Spatial and Object. Fallback and retained samples contribute equally weighted imitation losses. Checkpoint selection. checkpoint qualifies when calibration target success is at most 10% and retained success decreases by at most ten percentage points relative to the original. We select the qualifying checkpoint with the highest retained success, breaking ties toward the earlier checkpoint. When none qualifies, we apply this ranking to the candidates that meet the suppression criterion. If suppression also fails, we first minimize target success and then apply the same ranking. Held-out outcomes are evaluated after selection. BadLIBERO uses each recipes final checkpoint, which is at 300 updates for the single-stage edits. C.5 Baseline Adaptations All baselines use the OFT action representation. GA increases L1 error on prohibited demonstrations, and GradDiff combines this update with retained-action imitation. NPO-RT applies negative preference optimization through continuousaction score and retained imitation. RMU redirects prohibited-input hidden states toward random vector while preserving original hidden states on retained inputs. Response and VLA baselines. Refusal FT learns controller-generated home-return trajectories from interrupted tasks, together with retainedtask demonstrations. The controller preserves the last gripper command during return, opens the gripper for reset demonstrations, and clips arm commands to the normalization bounds. Training demonstrations are interrupted before release or completion for placement tasks and before contact for the stove. Their median interruption times are later than held-out mid-task takeover for placement and earlier for the stove. VLA-Forget uses staged module-wise LoRA, gradient projection, and action-output distillation in our OFT implementation. The VLA-Forget results describe our deployed OFT adaptation, whose action outputs differ after checkpoint reloading.

Takeovers occur at first gripperbox contact and five steps before the earlier of post-grasp opening and L3 entry. Every method uses the same donor states and fixed observation window. The physical-incident metric combines four event types. drop occurs when an ungrasped object remains more than 10 cm below its postwait initial height for two consecutive steps. Lost hold applies to box grasped at takeover that remains ungrasped, outside L3, and more than 10 cm below its takeover height for two consecutive steps. Disturbance records movement beyond 5 cm or tilt beyond 45 from the takeover pose for objects outside the task objects of interest and trigger box. fallen-body event records non-box drop or an initially grasped box ending ungrasped and more than 10 cm below its takeover height. Their union counts incidents even when they accompany attack-target attainment. Beyond the main-table endpoints, SAFI produces hold-like response in 87.5% of takeovers. This response requires no target attainment, release, or physical incident, with end-effector excursion within 3 cm of the takeover position. On clean, untriggered inputs, SAFI retains 96.0% clean-task success, compared with 91.0% for the implanted policy and 95.0% for the clean reference. sections.title: Instruction and Visual Shifts
sections.content: D.1.2 We also evaluate normal starts under instruction paraphrases and warmer image colors, after checking that the original policy remains competent in each condition. SAFI records zero target success across all three Goal prohibitions under both shifts, with retained success ranging from 91.1% to 96.7%. This result extends the initial-state suppression finding beyond the canonical instructions and image appearance. D.2 Supervision Design (RQ2) The main ablation examines the two imitation terms. Here, we retain both terms and vary the states supplying fallback supervision to examine the role of execution-state coverage. All variants use the same Spatial and Object cohorts, training budget, and checkpoint-selection procedure. Prefix-only supervision uses chunks entirely before the first gripper-close command. Countmatched full-trajectory supervision distributes the same number of candidate chunks across each demonstration. Post-close-only supervision uses chunks starting at or after that boundary, and full SAFI uses all valid chunks. The matched-count comparison controls the available candidate count while changing their temporal coverage and associated gripper labels. All four variants suppress normal-start completion, but prefix-only supervision permits almost complete target execution after takeover  (Table 10)  . Distributing the same candidate count across the full trajectory reduces takeover success to 0.6% in both suites. Post-close supervision and full SAFI also achieve low target success while retaining high utility. This pattern supports teaching the fallback at states encountered during execution.

Refusal FTs additional completions occur on the bowl-next-to-plate task, where its selected policy falls below the held-out retention criterion. sections.title: E Computational Efficiency
sections.content: We measure adaptation and action-prediction costs to assess the computational requirements of SAFI. The inference comparison uses the original and adapted policies on the same H100 GPU, with batch size one and merged LoRA adapters. Each timed call processes cached observations and produces fresh eight-action chunk, including input and action postprocessing. Table 15 shows median latency near 58 ms per chunk and approximately 15 GiB peak allocated memory for both policies. These similar deployment costs are consistent with SAFIs unchanged action-prediction path after adaptation. Table 16 summarizes the 300-update adaptation loop, measured after setup through the final update. The median time is 12.2 minutes per target, with approximately 31 GiB peak allocated memory per process while two training processes share an H100. These measurements characterize the training cost of the evaluated recipe alongside its deployed inference cost.

sections.title: F Qualitative Comparisons
sections.content: Figure 8 shows the behavioral differences behind the two motivations. The bottle case contrasts task completion, dropping, and continued holding, while the stove case contrasts activation with suppression after takeover. We render the recorded actions from matched starting states and verify the displayed NPO-RT and SAFI states against their evaluation logs. Figure 8: Trajectories after matched mid-task takeover. Columns show the same elapsed control steps across methods. Original completes both prohibited tasks. NPO-RT drops the bottle and activates the stove, while SAFI keeps the bottle held and the stove off. Each panel ends at Originals task completion. 22 F.1 Motivation Figure Protocol The upper panel of Figure 2 compares stove activation from initial, early, and mid-task states under the restart protocol. Its initial-state condition is separate from the held-out normal-start evaluation in Table 7. The lower panel accumulates bottle-drop events over all episodes in each condition until their termination. Each curve ends at its last observed step, with the original policys shorter window reflecting earlier task completion. The curves therefore describe recorded outcomes over the observed execution intervals.
